audit.recode_to: Not uniform 'fixed-dominant final'. Recode as a non-contrastive, lexically/etymologically conditioned system: final stress on Atayal-stratum words; Japanese-stratum words (c. 65% of basic vocabulary per Sanada 2013) penultimate when 3+ syllables and weight-sensitive (VV>Vn>VG>V, else free/lexical) when disyllabic (Lin 2021, Aohua); Tungyueh described as final~penult fluctuating (Sanada 2013 p.105). If the catalog must keep a single fixed class, at minimum set strict=false, add a caution 'final vs penult varies by lexical stratum and village; weight-sensitive disyllables reported for Aohua', cite Lin 2021 pp.55-58 and Sanada 2013 p.105 alongside Qiu 2015 p.39, and fix the locator to p.39.
audit.reasoning: Quote genuine (Qiu 2015 p.39, fetched sources now; nothing was held before). But the deciding source is a syntax-focused MA thesis whose stress claim rests on two words from one village (Hanhsi) plus an appeal to Atayal. Every other first-hand source I opened either qualifies or contradicts uniform final stress: Sanada 2013 (Tungyueh) final or penult, fluctuating; Lin 2021 (Aohua, the only dedicated stress study) final only for the Atayal stratum, penult for Japanese-stratum polysyllables and weight-sensitive for Japanese disyllables; Tan 2023 reports non-final patterns in her own data. Only Sanada & Chien 2012 p.42 supports plain final. Since the Japanese stratum is the majority of the lexicon, 'final-dominant' is unlikely to survive a re-read; hence at-risk / recode.
audit.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE CHECK (re-done on the fetched sources file, 85 pp): extracted text of pdf p.49 carries running header '39' and contains sec. 6.1.3, sec. 6.1.4 'Stress' and the start of 6.2; pdf p.50 is headed '40' and begins 'The third-person pronoun'. Sec. 6.1.4 reads verbatim: 'Stress normally falls on the final syllable in Yilan Creole, as seen in [waha] 'I' (ED) (J) and [lalaŋ] 'before' (ED; A). This feature derives from Atayal, which is known to be a stress-final language (Li, 1980, p. 356), whereas Japanese is a pitch-accent language (Tsujimura, 2007) in which the location of a word's accent is not predicable.' Foo

sources.citation: Tan, Gan-ling. 2023. A new view on 'Yilan Creole'. Journal of Pidgin and Creole Languages 38(2): 320-388. doi:10.1075/jpcl.00115.tan (CC BY 4.0).
sources.quote: 'according to Qiu (2015: 39), stress in Vernacular Atayalic Japanese always falls on the final syllable of the word regardless of the word's origin ... However, my data show that in Vernacular Atayalic Japanese words in isolation can have non-word-final stress patterns. Due to limited space, I will discuss this issue in a separate paper.'
sources.note: Glottolog's top-ranked description (69 pp, OA); p.337 explicitly disputes Qiu's uniform final stress from the author's own fieldwork.

sources.citation: Sanada, Shinji & Chien, Yuehchen. 2012. Giran kureōru [Yilan Creole]. Kokugoken purojekuto rebyū / NINJAL Project Review 3(1): 38-48.
sources.quote: アクセントは非弁別的で，最後の音節に置かれる。これはアタヤル語のアクセントと同様である。 [Accent is non-distinctive and placed on the last syllable; this is the same as Atayal accent.]
sources.note: Project overview by the primary describers; p.42 states accent non-distinctive and final (the one independent confirmation of our coding).

sources.citation: Lin, Kaidi. 2021. The stress system in the Aohua dialect of Yilan Creole: with a special focus on weight-sensitivity. Proceedings of the 162nd Meeting of the Linguistic Society of Japan, A-8, pp.54-60.
sources.quote: 'Atayal-originated words of any length have ultimate fixed stress (I). Japanese-originated words have different stress positions depending on the number of syllables': monosyllables trivially; 'three or more syllables, the stress will be on the penultimate syllable' (karara, kuruma, kucibiru); 'Disyllabic words of Japanese origin have a weight-sensitive stress system ... VV > Vn > VG > V ... If both syllables have the same syllable weight, the stress can appear on either, or is lexically determined.' Notes Tongyueh (Sanada 2013: final or penult) and Hanhsi (Qiu 2015: final) and says other dial
sources.locator: sec. 4-4.2, pp.55-58; sec. 4.4 p.59 on other dialects
sources.note: The only dedicated description of Yilan Creole word stress from first-hand field data; reports origin-split final~penult plus weight-sensitive disyllables, against our uniform 'final-dominant' coding that rests on two words in a syntax MA thesis.

sources.citation: Qiu, Peng. 2015. A preliminary investigation of Yilan Creole in Taiwan: discussing predicate position in Yilan Creole. MA thesis, University of Alberta. 85 pp.
sources.quote: Stress normally falls on the final syllable in Yilan Creole, as seen in [waha] 'I' (ED)(J) and [lalaŋ] 'before' (ED; A). This feature derives from Atayal, which is known to be a stress-final language (Li, 1980, p. 356).

sources.citation: Sanada, Shinji. 2013. Giran kureōru no on'in oboegaki [Notes on Yilan Creole phonology]. Sōgō seisaku kenkyū (Kwansei Gakuin) 44: 103-105.
sources.quote: アクセントは非弁別的で、語末の音節、乃至語末から2番目の音節に置かれる。ただし、両者で音韻的な対立は存在しない。…宜蘭クレオールでは、個人的に、かつ個人の中においても、アクセントの置かれる位置が、語によって、語末と語末から2番目の音節とで揺れる傾向 [Accent is non-distinctive, placed on the final or the penultimate syllable, with no phonological opposition; position fluctuates between final and penult by word, across and within speakers; penult attributed to Seediq residue].
sources.locator: sec. 4 'アクセント', p.105 (Tungyueh village, male b.1964)
sources.note: First-hand phonology note on the Tungyueh variety by the language's principal describer: accent final OR penultimate, fluctuating, non-contrastive; qualifies 'final-dominant'.
